claims.text: Interpretive nutrient-specific front-of-package labels significantly decrease consumers' attention to the Nutrition Facts Panel.
Interpretive summary indicator labels significantly decrease consumers' attention to the Nutrition Facts Panel.
Interpretive nutrient-specific labels increase consumers' overall healthfulness perceptions of food products.
Interpretive nutrient-specific labels increase the perceived healthfulness of vice products.
Interpretive labels negatively influence consumers' tastiness evaluations of labeled products.
Interpretive summary indicator labels improve consumers' ability to identify healthier food options.
Front-of-package labels have positive but smaller effects on healthy choice compared to the identification of healthy options.
Front-of-package labels have no statistically significant overall effect on actual food consumption across all three label types.
Health claims significantly increase consumers' purchase intentions toward vice products carrying those claims.
Consumers are less influenced by front-of-package labels when evaluating the healthfulness of known brands compared to fictitious or unknown brands.

evidence.description: Random-effects HOMA meta-analysis found r = -.104 (p < .05, k = 39) for interpretive nutrient-specific labels on attention to NFP.
Random-effects HOMA meta-analysis showed r = -.259 (p < .001, k = 1) for interpretive summary indicators on attention to NFP.
Random-effects HOMA reported an overall effect size of r = .051 (p < .001, k = 318) for interpretive nutrient-specific labels on healthfulness perceptions.
Interpretive nutrient-specific labels showed r = .030 (p < .01, k = 153) on healthfulness perceptions of vice products.

HOMA results showed tastiness perceptions were negatively affected by interpretive nutrient-specific labels (r = -.160, p < .001, k = 88) and interpretive summary indicators (r = -.166, p < .01, k = 29).
HOMA meta-analysis showed r = .374 (p < .001, k = 66) for interpretive summary indicator labels on healthy identification.

Healthy choice correlations were r = .093 (reductive nutrient-specific), r = .079 (interpretive nutrient-specific), and r = .023 (interpretive summary), markedly lower than identification correlations of r = .266, r = .177, and r = .374.

Random-effects HOMA revealed nonsignificant overall effects on consumption for reductive nutrient-specific (r = -.008, k = 6), interpretive nutrient-specific (r = .036, k = 50), and interpretive summary indicator labels (r = .006, k = 13).
HOMA results indicated health claims had a significant positive effect on purchase intention for vice products (r = .139, p < .001, k = 11).
HiLMA regression showed that brand familiarity had a negative moderating effect on healthfulness perceptions (beta = -.048, p < .001).

methodologies.name: Random-effects Hedges-Olkin Meta-Analysis (HOMA)
methodologies.description: Weighted random-effects meta-analysis transforming correlation coefficients via Fisher's Zr to estimate mean effect sizes across labels and outcomes.
datasets: 1594 effect sizes from 114 articles (130 studies) published between 1996 and 2018
conditions: Fisher's Zr transformed correlation coefficients weighted by inverse variance (N - 3)

methodologies.name: Hierarchical Linear Meta-Analysis (HiLMA)
methodologies.description: Weighted hierarchical regression model accounting for within-study effect size dependency and assessing moderating product, consumer, and study factors.
conditions: Clustered by publication to handle correlated errors

methodologies.name: Crowdsourced Vice-Virtue Category Rating Survey
methodologies.description: Survey assessing perceived vice vs. virtue ratings of 78 food product categories on a 9-point Likert scale.

limitations.text: Prior meta-analyses were restricted to specific FOP labels (such as health claims only) or limited sets of outcomes (such as healthy choice and consumption only).
Many relevant identified studies were excluded from the meta-analysis due to unavailable or non-retrievable data.
The analysis filters only the most common methodological choices, missing other study characteristics that could introduce bias.
All included primary studies assume consumer awareness of the label, whereas attention and motivation at point-of-purchase vary in real retail environments.
Certain outcome measures, specifically attention to the NFP for summary indicators and attitude measures, were based on very few effect sizes.

future_work.text: Investigate whether front-of-package label formats influence consumers with differing levels of health consciousness or nutrition knowledge.
Examine how label design features (such as shape, coloring, abstractness, and placement) impact attentional capture and consumer choice.
Examine the simultaneous influence of multiple front-of-package labels and their interaction with other package claims.
Examine the systemic effects of front-of-package labeling on manufacturer recipe reformulation and retailer assortment decisions.
